elements.element: The licence extends to Customer's affiliates.
elements.evidence: Grant now runs to "Company and its affiliates (on written notice to Contractor)"; "Company" is defined in the preamble as Clear Capital only, so the added words supply genuinely new affiliate coverage rather than duplicating an existing definition.

elements.element: The licence extends to contractors acting on Customer's behalf.
elements.evidence: Section 4(c) as rendered names only "Company and its affiliates"; no words extend the grant to contractors or other third parties acting on Company's behalf. The pre-existing sublicensing right is a discretionary right to grant sublicences, not an express licence to Company's contractors.
Retained language grants a "royalty-free, non-exclusive perpetual license" — the licence is fully paid-up (royalty-free) and expressly perpetual.
The grant says "royalty-free, non-exclusive perpetual" but nowhere says "irrevocable"; the drafter would need to insert "irrevocable" into the string of licence adjectives in Section 4(c).

elements.element: A subscription licence is terminable only for uncured material breach.
elements.evidence: Conditional element whose condition does not apply: the only licence in the document is a royalty-free perpetual grant of Contractor's Information incorporated into the Works; there is no subscription or term-limited licence for this restriction to attach to.

elements.element: The licence is transferable to Customer's successors.
elements.evidence: The insertion is limited to "a successor in a merger or acquisition without Contractor's approval". Read literally that is narrower than transferability to Customer's successors generally (e.g. successor by asset sale, reorganisation or operation of law); the drafter would need to broaden to "transferable to Customer's successors and assigns" for the preferred element.

elements.element: Customer's affiliates are covered on written notice.
elements.evidence: "Contractor hereby grants to Company and its affiliates (on written notice to Contractor) a royalty-free, non-exclusive perpetual license" — affiliate coverage with the written-notice mechanic exactly as the fallback requires.

elements.element: The licence is transferable to a successor in a merger or acquisition transaction.
elements.evidence: "transferable to a successor in a merger or acquisition without Contractor's approval" is inserted into the operative grant, and the express no-approval wording neutralises the general consent requirement in Section 10 for this transfer.

reasons: Fallback checklist is complete in operative language: affiliate coverage on written notice and M&A successor transferability are both inside the Section 4(c) grant, not merely promised in the margin comment.

Preferred level fails on three elements: no contractor coverage, no "irrevocable", and successor transferability narrowed to M&A only. To reach preferred the drafter would add "and its contractors acting on its behalf", insert "irrevocable" among the licence adjectives, and broaden "a successor in a merger or acquisition" to Customer's successors generally.

Minimality holds: only the two fallback features were added to an existing grant; the favourable retained terms (royalty-free, non-exclusive, perpetual, sublicensable, business-operations scope) are untouched, nothing outside the checklist (no survival tail, expense or procedure language) is added, and no word was deleted.
The "without Contractor's approval" tag is the permitted direct form rather than a broad notwithstanding override of Section 10, so it does not breach the minimality boundary on assignment overrides.

Intent preserved: Section 10 is left intact and is not contradicted — it governs assignment of the Agreement and its obligations, whereas the new words permit transfer of a specific licence right; no new assignment exception is granted to Contractor, and no undefined term or dangling cross-reference is created ("affiliates" is used in its ordinary sense, consistent with the Agreement's undefined usage).
Minor drafting nit for the record, not a failure: "a successor" is unqualified as to which party's successor; "a successor to Company" would remove any ambiguity.
